kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-02.title: Use the middle number
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-02.body:
The five numbers are evenly spaced around 2003, so their sum is $5 \times 2003 = 10015$.

**Answer: (E) 10015**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-03.title: Compare the two routes
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-03.body:
The detour goes 3 km down, then along a stretch exactly as long as A'B', then 3 km back up. The middle part is the same length as the road it replaces, so the extra distance is $3 + 3 = 6$ km.

**Answer: (C) 6 km**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-03.title: The length of A'B' doesn't matter
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-03.body:
Call the length of A'B' $x$ km. The normal road there is $x$ km; the detour is $3 + x + 3 = x + 6$ km. Whatever $x$ is, the detour is 6 km longer.

**Answer: (C) 6 km**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-04.title: The difference never changes
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-04.body:
When his sister was born, Jerome was 4 years older than her. Both get one year older every year, so the difference always stays 4 years.

**Answer: (A) 4 years**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-04.title: Work out the sister's age
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-04.body:
Jerome is 9 now, and his sister was born 4 years after him, so she is $9 - 4 = 5$. Difference: $9 - 5 = 4$ years.

**Answer: (A) 4 years**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-07.title: Compare with eating half of everything
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-07.body:
If Joseph had eaten half of the apples and half of the oranges, exactly half of all the fruits would remain. But he ate only one third of the oranges, which is less than half, so more oranges remain than in that case. So more than half of all fruits remain.

**Answer: (B) more than half of all fruits**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-07.title: Try numbers
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-07.body:
Say there are 6 apples and 6 oranges (12 fruits). He eats 3 apples and 2 oranges, so $12 - 5 = 7$ fruits remain — more than half of 12. Any numbers give the same result, because half of the apples stay and more than half of the oranges stay.

**Answer: (B) more than half of all fruits**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-08.title: Red must be one third of all squares
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-08.body:
The grid has $6 \times 4 = 24$ squares, 5 of them red. If red is half of yellow, then for every 1 red there are 2 yellow, so red is one third of all squares: $24 \div 3 = 8$. We need $8 - 5 = 3$ more red squares.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-08.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-08.body:
Paint 3 squares red: 8 red and 16 yellow, and 8 is half of 16 ✓. Painting 2 would give 7 red and 17 yellow; painting 4 would give 9 red and 15 yellow — neither works.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-11.title: Remove pencils from both sides
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-11.body:
On the first scale there are 7 pencils on the left and 2 pencils plus 30 g on the right. Taking 2 pencils from each side keeps it balanced: 5 pencils = 30 g, so one pencil weighs 6 g. On the second scale, pencil + pen = 15 g, so the pen weighs $15 - 6 = 9$ g.

**Answer: (D) 9 g**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-11.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-11.body:
If a pencil weighs 6 g: left side $7 \times 6 = 42$ g, right side $2 \times 6 + 30 = 42$ g ✓. Then pen $= 15 - 6 = 9$ g.

**Answer: (D) 9 g**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-13.title: Place blue, then red, then green
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-13.body:
The even numbers are 2 and 4, so blue is #2 or #4 and yellow is the other one. The red house has only one neighbour (the blue one), so it is at an end: #1 next to blue #2, or #5 next to blue #4. Green is on the other side of blue: if blue is #2, green is #3; if blue is #4, green is #3. Either way house #3 is green.

**Answer: (E) Green**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-13.title: Rule out colours for #3
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-13.body:
#3 is odd, so it is not blue or yellow. Red is at an end (it has only one neighbour), so it is not #3. Blue (at #2 or #4) has red on one side and green on the other; the other side of blue from the end is #3. So #3 is green, and pink is the remaining end house.

**Answer: (E) Green**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-14.title: Total of the table
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-14.body:
Adding the two rows gives the sum of all four numbers: $3 + 8 = 11$. The first column has 4 of that, so the second column has $11 - 4 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-14.title: Try an example
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-14.body:
For instance, first row 1 and 2 (sum 3), second row 3 and 5 (sum 8). The first column is $1 + 3 = 4$ ✓, and the second column is $2 + 5 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-15.title: Add odd numbers
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-15.body:
Each new figure adds a new row along the bottom: 1, then $1 + 3 = 4$, then $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$. The fourth figure has $9 + 7 = 16$ and the fifth $16 + 9 = 25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-15.title: Square numbers
kangaroo-ca-2011-training-g0304-15.body:
1, 4, 9 are $1 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$, $3 \times 3$. The fifth figure has $5 \times 5 = 25$ triangles.

**Answer: (C) 25**
